newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic plays old cat-and-mouse game - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic plays old cat-and-mouse game - analysts.

text.p: President Slobodan Milosevic, fighting off democratic pressures in Serbia and from abroad, is applying similar tactics to those he used in Bosnia -- delaying, dissembling and exploiting the West's lack of unity.
"It is the same old game of cat-and-mouse for Milosevic. Delay, prevaricate, break promises and deadlines, and confuse the hell out of everyone," a senior Western diplomat said on Thursday.

He was referring to the two-month-old political crisis in Serbia which erupted after Milosevic's ruling Socialists and neo-communists annulled election victories by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition in 14 cities including Belgrade.
What the ruling parties thought would be a routine operation failed dismally when Zajedno refused to surrender and rallied hundreds of thousands of supporters into the streets.
In a way, they resembled Bosnia's Moslems who did not lie down in 1992 when faced with the superior firepower of a Bosnian Serb army organized, financed and supplied by Milosevic.
"There is a strong sense of deja vu here. There are many similarities between Milosevic's modus operandi in Serbia now and in Bosnia then," the diplomat said.
Milosevic and his Bosnian Serb proxies exploited the disunity of the major Western powers and Russia to overrun 70 percent of Bosnia early in the 1992-95 war.

Only when the powers closed ranks with air strikes against Serb forces in pursuit of peace did Milosevic accept a U.S.-brokered settlement in Dayton, Ohio under which Serbs had to roll back to just half of Bosnia's territory.
Milosevic was reported to have agreed to acknowledge Zajedno's election wins last Friday and again on Sunday under great pressure from the West and nine-week-old demonstrations.
But political sources said Milosevic was convinced he won more time after the Contact Group powers decided on Saturday not to impose fresh sanctions on Belgrade for the time being.
Throughout Bosnia's war, Serbs never respected U.N. or NATO deadlines for compliance with peace steps, earning Milosevic a sobriquet: "The master of brinksmanship".
They always came around in reaction to post-deadline bombings by NATO planes but gave up as little as possible, rarely fulfilling all international demands.
On Tuesday, city election commissions reinstated Zajedno's victories in Belgrade and the second largest Serbian city Nis, but the other cities at issue remained on hold.
Europe's biggest security body called on Belgrade on Thursday to forget paltry solutions.

"Step-by-step concessions to the opposition on what ought to be a merely mechanical issue -- translating the results into seats -- is simply not the way to handle this situation," said Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, chairman in office of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
As in Bosnia against the Moslems, Milosevic's hardliners are threatening force against opponents, occasionally giving them a taste of violence despite promises to restrain the police.
Western diplomats said Belgrade had assured the United States that it would "positively solve the crisis by January 12." That did not happen.
An OSCE meeting in Vienna passed on Thursday without any punishment threatened against Belgrade. U.S. proposals for renewed sanctions were rejected by European allies.
The next diplomatic stages in the saga will be a European Union ministerial meeting in a few days and the inauguration of U.S. President Bill Clinton on January 20.
But diplomats noted that Milosevic's game in Bosnia ended in loss when he gave up more territory to his adversaries than he would have had to if the Serbs had accepted a deal in 1993.

"Milosevic's regime will ultimately, under pressure, accept anything but as a rule at a much higher price than if they had accepted a deal in the first place," said Dragoslav Avramovic, the reformist former Yugoslav National Bank governor.

Serbia, still reeling from four years of U.N. sanctions and war costs, is facing economic disaster unless it urgently gets an infusion of fresh capital. The West is adamant in withholding funds until Milosevic toes the line.

"The current political crisis has long eclipsed the reason which provoked it, but the immense damage to Serbia testifies to a foolish, irresponsible policy," Dusan Mihajlovic, the leader of the moderate New Democracy Party, allied in the ruling coalition, told Reuters on Thursday.
"We have a saying: "You don't kill a whole ox for a pound of beef,'" he added.
